sections.h2: Selling a house in Livingston, NJ
sections.html:
Livingston is a high-value Essex County township, so the biggest costs in a sale tend to be the price-based state fees and whatever repairs a buyer's inspector flags. The local to-do list is brief: get a smoke detector certification from the fire department and find out whether any building permits remain open. The rest is the deed, the state fee tables and Essex County recording.

The township covers 13.79 square miles of land and had an estimated 32,223 residents in mid-2025. The 2020 count of 31,330 was the highest it has recorded. Owners live in 88.9% of homes, and the middle owned home is worth $821,100, which puts a typical sale in one of the upper brackets of the state fee schedule.

Place names buyers use include Cheapside, Northfield, Washington Place, West Livingston and Cedar Ridge. The township borders Roseland to the north, West Orange to the east, Millburn and Short Hills to the south, and Florham Park and East Hanover in Morris County to the west.

Commutes average 37.6 minutes, which makes highway and bus access a real selling point. The township is 21.9 miles from New York City, and rail service runs through stations in neighboring communities.

  • Highways: Interstate 280 and Route 10 cross the town, and I-80, the Parkway and the Turnpike are reached via I-280.
  • Bus to Manhattan: the Community Coach 77 line runs to Port Authority, and OurBus operates a commuter route serving Livingston and West Orange.
  • Bus to Newark: NJ Transit routes 70, 71 and 73, with local route 873.
  • Rail: Morristown Line stations in Short Hills, Millburn and South Orange sit 5 to 7 miles away, and the fee-based Livingston Express Shuttle makes a 15-minute run between Livingston Mall and South Orange Station.

sections.h2: Do you need a C.O. to sell in Livingston?
sections.html:
No. The township does not require a certificate of occupancy for a sale. It does recommend phoning the Building Department (973-992-5000, extension 5200) to see whether any permits are still open on the property, and to call well ahead of closing because open permits can hold up a sale. The department is at 357 S. Livingston Avenue, second floor.

A smoke detector certification is required, and the Livingston Fire Department issues it at 973-992-2373. The Fire Prevention Bureau also inspects residential properties at resale or when a rental changes hands, and it enforces the state fire code for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.

Township permit rules shape the questions a buyer's attorney will raise, so check these:

  • Replacing a sink, toilet or tub in the same spot needs no permit, but moving fixtures does.
  • New electrical or plumbing work needs a permit even when you only swap cabinets.
  • Sheds larger than 200 square feet need a building permit plus zoning approval; smaller ones need zoning approval only.
  • Fences enclosing a pool, spa or hot tub need a building permit.

The seller pays the state's transfer fee when the deed is recorded. At $821,100, a typical Livingston sale reaches the $550,000 to $850,000 band of the over-$350,000 schedule, charged at $5.30 per $500 for that slice, with lower bands applying to the dollars beneath it.

Above $1 million, a graduated fee applies to residential deeds, starting at 1% of the whole price and rising to 3.5% for prices over $3.5 million. The seller owes it, and the deed must carry the state's affidavit form (RTF-1EE). Run the number before you accept an offer close to that line.

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records deeds for all 22 Essex municipalities, Livingston included. Your closing attorney or title company normally handles the filing, so you rarely visit the office yourself. If you are an executor distributing an inherited house to an heir, the state's exemption list covers a deed from an executor or administrator to a devisee or heir, though a sale to an outside buyer is a normal taxable transfer.

sections.h2: Schools, parks and shopping that shape demand
sections.html:
Many buyers start their search with schools. Livingston Public Schools have six elementary schools (Burnet Hill, Collins, Harrison, Hillside, Mount Pleasant and Riker Hill), Mount Pleasant Middle School for grade 6, Heritage Middle School for grades 7 and 8, and Livingston High School.

Roughly a quarter of the township's land stays in a natural state, with more than 470 acres of wooded parkland and trails. The Livingston Mall has lost several anchors, while the Route 10 corridor and the Livingston Town Center mixed-use project carry more everyday shopping.

Once a buyer signs, the closing attorney orders the title search and asks you for the deed, your mortgage payoff and proof of the smoke detector certification. Book the fire department visit as soon as you list, because a missed appointment can push a closing date back a week or more. If the Building Department turns up an open permit, you have two choices: finish and close it, or tell the buyer and negotiate a credit.

At the table you sign the deed and the state's seller forms. Your attorney deducts the transfer fee and the loan payoff, splits the open tax quarter with the buyer and hands over the balance. A cash buyer shortens the path by dropping the lender's appraisal and conditions, though every item above still applies.

sections.h2: Listing or selling as-is in Livingston
sections.html:
Where the typical home is worth more than $800,000, a house that is updated and shows well gives a listing room to work. An as-is sale fits better when the house needs a roof, kitchen or systems work, when you have a fixed moving date, or when you inherited the property and want a quick close.

Judge each offer by what lands in your pocket. Take off the transfer fee, repairs a buyer will demand, carrying costs during a listing period and the smoke certification, and insist on written offers.

Before any offer, call the Fire Department for the smoke certification, ask the Building Department about open permits, and give your closing attorney the deed and mortgage payoff details. With those three items in hand, paperwork seldom holds up a Livingston closing, and you can focus on comparing price and terms across offers, including who bears each fee and how soon the money arrives.

faqs.q: Does Livingston require a C.O. before a sale?
faqs.a: No. A smoke detector certification from the fire department is required, and the Building Department can tell you about open permits, ideally well ahead of closing.

faqs.q: Where do I get Livingston's smoke detector certification?
faqs.a: Phone the Livingston Fire Department at 973-992-2373. Its Fire Prevention Bureau covers detector compliance when residential properties are resold.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee a seller cost in Livingston?
faqs.a: Yes. The state computes it from the price stated in the deed and collects it at recording. Sales above $1 million also carry a graduated percent fee, which the seller owes.

faqs.q: Which office records a Livingston deed?
faqs.a: The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which serves all 22 county municipalities. A closing attorney or title agent usually files the deed.

faqs.q: What if my Livingston house has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: You can still sell, but expect questions. Call the Building Department at 973-992-5000, extension 5200, to learn what is on file; a buyer's lender or attorney may want the work permitted or reflected in the price.
